title: In-the-money call spreads on a sold-off stock with high implied volatility
summary: When a stock is getting crushed and implied volatility rises, the speaker buys an in-the-money call spread, which he says is economically the same as selling an out-of-the-money put spread. His Netflix example: at support, RSI low, below moving averages. A one-month spread gives long delta, positive carry if nothing happens, and short vega while IV is high.

steps.caption: Netflix after a selloff, at support and below its moving averages. The $90 price and strikes are illustrative.
A: buy the $80 call, sell the $85 call, one month out. Both strikes are in the money: you get long delta.
B: sell the $85 put, buy the $80 put. The speaker says the two trades are economically the same.
Breakeven sits below the current price: positive carry, you make money if nothing happens.
As time passes with the price unchanged, the spread moves toward its maximum.
Short vega: with IV high, a fall in implied volatility acts as a tailwind.

takeaways: When a stock is getting crushed and IV is rising, an in-the-money call spread is one of the speaker's favorite structures.
He says buying the ITM call spread and selling the OTM put spread are economically the same; he prefers the call spread.
The structure is long delta, positive carry, and short vega when implied volatility is high.
His rule of thumb: be short vega when IV is high and long vega when IV is low.
caveats: The speaker says it is not a trade recommendation. Netflix's price and the strikes here are illustrative; he gives none.
Earnings were a couple of weeks away, which he says affects his VAY score. VAY is the speaker's promotional metric.
Added context: if the stock ends below the lower strike at expiry, the full debit is lost.

backtest.note: One-month call spread with both strikes in the money. Deltas, profit take and stop are assumptions; the speaker gives no exit rules.
